newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD presses for early German tax shakeup.
newsitem.headline: SPD presses for early German tax shakeup.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Wednesday they might drop their opposition to the government's planned tax reforms if a partial shakeup of the tax system is brought into force this October.
But, finance spokeswoman Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier told Berlin radio, the SPD would not support any changes which would increase the tax burden on Germans.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government is trying to square the circle of containing borrowing this year to qualify for Europe's single currency, while plotting a tax-cutting reform to be completed by 1999 to boost growth and fight unemployment.

Both efforts risk being blocked by the SPD-led upper house of parliament, and fellow opposition party the Greens warned SPD-ruled states in the chamber against giving in to pressure from the government.

"The opposition is not there to help the government out of its fix by making sloppy compromises," Greens spokeswoman Kerstin Mueller said in Bonn. Any SPD-government deal could endanger chances of building a "red-green" coalition at the general election to be held in October 1998, she added.

One idea being mulled by the coalition is to bring forward parts of its two-stage tax reform from 1999 to 1998 -- although critics say that by seeking to scrap tax breaks before cutting taxes the government is actually planning effective tax hikes.
Matthaeus-Maier repeated earlier SPD demands to cut occupational insurance charges from this October, with the cost to be covered by a moderate increase in petrol tax.

She also said the government could not afford to meet its pledge to cut the so-called solidarity surcharge -- a tax raised to help finance German unification -- by two percentage points next year at a cost of 7.5 billion marks.
"The coalition should say honestly: the money is not there," Matthaeus-Maier said.
